title: Not just Neanderthals: Ghost lineage in Africa left its mark on our DNA
gist: A Berkeley-led team built a tool called TRACE that spots introgressed DNA by its signature of looking old in ancestry but young in recombination, validated it on known Neanderthal and Denisovan sequences, and then found a third, unsampled "ghost" lineage that interbred with humans in Africa before the out-of-Africa expansion. It contributes roughly 0.5–1.1 percent of current genomes, collectively covering nearly 1.5 billion bases, and split from us over 800,000 years ago; a separate superarchaic signal, ~1.8 million years old, entered via Denisovans.

insights.claim: DNA introgressed from a separate hominin lineage carries a distinctive dual signature — bases whose common ancestry traces very far back, yet which show unusually little recombination — and this two-part test is the operating principle of the new TRACE software tool.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: A reusable detection principle that can find interbreeding partners for which no fossil genome exists, expanding what population genomics can claim without new ancient DNA.
insights.quote: Many of its bases should look “old” in the sense of how far back their common ancestry can be traced, yet they should look “young” in terms of how much recombination has taken place.

insights.claim: TRACE is built on ancestral recombination graphs, which estimate for every base in a genome how many generations back it first appeared and how often it has been involved in recombination.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: ARG reconstruction is the compute-heavy substrate this whole class of discovery now depends on — a bottleneck and an opportunity for genomics tooling.
insights.locator: With enough genomic data, computers can be used

insights.claim: The method tolerates a high per-base error rate because averaging inferences across the human genome's three billion bases makes the aggregate picture informative even when many individual histories are wrong.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Explains why noisy ARG inference is still usable — the same noise-averaging logic underwrites confidence in the ghost-lineage result.
insights.locator: Because of the randomness of some of these things

insights.claim: Tested against already-identified Neanderthal and Denisovan sequences, TRACE achieved over 90 percent accuracy with a false discovery rate below a quarter of a percent.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: The error floor is far below the size of the new signal it reports, which is what makes the ghost-lineage claim credible rather than an artifact.
insights.locator: To test the tool, they had convenient examples

insights.claim: Run on African populations, which only acquired Neanderthal and Denisovan DNA via back-migration from Eurasia, TRACE reported just 0.1 percent archaic ancestry — a negative control consistent with its low false-positive rate.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Confirms the tool does not manufacture archaic ancestry where little should exist, strengthening the separate ghost-lineage detection in the same populations.
insights.locator: In another demonstration, the researchers performed the analysis on African populations

insights.claim: Applying TRACE to about 500 modern human genomes revealed DNA from a previously unsampled ghost lineage making up roughly 0.5 to 1.1 percent of current human genomes.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Establishes a third archaic contributor to modern humans on top of Neanderthals and Denisovans, rewriting the standard two-partner story of human admixture.

insights.claim: Although each individual carries only about 1 percent ghost-lineage DNA, the segments collectively span nearly 1.5 billion bases — roughly half the three-billion-base human genome.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Enough of the vanished lineage's sequence is recoverable across people to reconstruct much of a genome that has no fossil source.
insights.locator: The percentage was small, at about 0.5 to 1.1 percent

insights.claim: Ghost-lineage DNA is present in all modern human populations, which places the interbreeding event before the out-of-Africa expansion.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Universality is the dating argument — it pins the encounter to Africa and to a period predating every known Neanderthal or Denisovan admixture.
insights.locator: It was present in all modern human populations

insights.claim: African populations carry more diverse and partly distinct ghost-lineage segments, and about 100 genomic regions contain no ghost-lineage DNA at all in non-African populations — a fingerprint of the diversity lost in the Eurasian founder event.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Non-African genome panels systematically undersample archaic variation, an argument for African-genome-heavy reference datasets in medical genomics.
insights.locator: But African populations carry more diverse segments

insights.claim: The ghost lineage last shared a common ancestor with modern humans over 800,000 years ago, making its divergence roughly contemporaneous with the split that produced Neanderthals and Denisovans.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Implies a third deep hominin branch coexisting in Africa, so the archaic human family tree had at least three surviving branches at admixture time.
insights.locator: Based on the last common ancestor of the sequences

insights.claim: Ghost-lineage segments are on average shorter than Neanderthal and Denisovan segments, indicating longer residence in the human genome and therefore an earlier introgression date.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Segment length works as an independent molecular clock corroborating the pre-out-of-Africa timing without any fossil evidence.
insights.locator: The segments in the human genome are, on average, shorter

insights.claim: Ghost-lineage DNA is found inside the genomic "deserts" that exclude Neanderthal and Denisovan DNA entirely, undercutting the idea that those regions simply cannot tolerate any divergent archaic variants.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Shifts the explanation for deserts from generic intolerance to specific incompatibility with Neanderthal/Denisovan alleles, redirecting hybrid-incompatibility research.
insights.quote: So there seems to be something actively problematic with the DNA from those lineages in these regions.
insights.locator: The modern human genome has areas, called “deserts,”

insights.claim: About 0.3 percent of the Denisovan DNA carried by genomes from Oceania traces back to a superarchaic lineage that branched from the modern human line nearly 1.8 million years ago, potentially Homo erectus or a similar ancestor.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Documents second-hand archaic ancestry — DNA reaching modern humans through an intermediate species — which complicates any simple accounting of human admixture.
insights.quote: And it apparently comes from a lineage that branched off from ours nearly 1.8 million years ago.

insights.claim: Archaic introgressed sequences are less common near genes, and the nearby genes that do exist often relate to metabolism and immune function, but the study does not establish that these ancient variants are adaptive.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Tempering signal: the functional or biomedical payoff of archaic variants remains speculative, so treat adaptive-introgression claims cautiously.
insights.locator: The work doesn’t really get into the significance

insights.claim: Nothing can currently be said about the ghost lineage beyond the fact that human ancestors encountered it in Africa, since no genome from it exists and the identification rests entirely on statistical inference from living people's DNA.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: The open question is whether ancient DNA or archaeology can ever attach a fossil to this lineage — the next headline in this research line.
insights.quote: the source of this DNA remains a “ghost lineage.”
insights.locator: Still, we now have samples of a fair amount of its DNA
